A Cheap Verifier is Good Enough: LLM Post-training is Robust to Erroneous Rewards

Andreas Plesner Affiliation: ETH Zurich Affiliation: Handshake AI    Curtis Northcutt Affiliation: Handshake AI    Francisco Guzmán Affiliation: Handshake AI    Anish Athalye Affiliation: Handshake AI
Abstract

When post-training large language models on tasks with semi-verifiable rewards, there are many factors (training steps, base model size, training order, data quality, verifier accuracy, etc.) that practitioners must contend with to maximize model performance. Yet, it remains unclear how well verifier agreement predicts post-training performance on such tasks. In this paper, we explore this question with over 11k H100 GPU-hours, across HealthBench and PRBench tasks in medical, legal, and finance domains. Across the tested domains, Qwen3 trainees (1.7B–8B on HealthBench; 8B on PRBench), evaluation splits, and frontier LLM reference judges (which we call golden verifiers), higher verifier agreement does not consistently identify the best training verifier. Expensive verifiers need not outperform inexpensive ones, and open-weight Gemma verifiers produce strong training outcomes. We compare two low-cost choices retrospectively — a cost-reducing choice and a balanced choice — with estimated grading cost reductions of 98.8%98.8\%–99.7%99.7\% relative to the golden grading protocols and average post-training score gaps of 11–33 points from the best evaluated training verifier. These averages include larger losses in individual settings; they do not establish that verifier choices are interchangeable.

1 Introduction

Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) has become the post-training method of choice for eliciting reasoning capabilities in Large Language Models (Shao et al., 2024; DeepSeek-AI, 2025; The Microsoft AI Team, 2026; Kimi Team et al., 2026; DeepSeek-AI et al., 2026). Early work focused on domains such as mathematics and coding, where deterministic checks provide a near-perfect reward signal (Austin et al., 2021). The field has since expanded from verifiable rewards to semi-verifiable rubric-based rewards for post-training. This extension allows training objectives to incorporate preferences and answer style alongside correctness. A verifier (sometimes called a grader or judge) is used to score task outputs according to a rubric composed of criteria (Gunjal et al., 2025; He et al., 2025; Viswanathan et al., 2025; Zhou et al., 2025; Lau et al., 2026). In some cases, these verifiers are used directly to provide rewards for post-training, where a natural hypothesis is that the accuracy of the rewards given by the verifier has a significant impact on the final performance of the post-trained model, especially in challenging domains with semi-verifiable rewards where taste preferences come into play.

This hypothesis has a natural human corollary: if Student A has a TA who grades their homework 30%30\% incorrectly and Student B has a “better” TA who grades their homework 10%10\% incorrectly, the common hypothesis is that Student B is likely to learn better over the course of the semester. Across the models we post-train (students), datasets (course material), verifiers (TAs), and golden verifiers (imperfect answer keys), better agreement with the answer key does not always identify the TA whose students learn most. Agreement remains informative, particularly for identifying very weak verifiers, but does not fully determine training outcomes. Our practical question is whether inexpensive verifiers can deliver strong post-training performance within a candidate pool that also includes strong, expensive models.

While prior work has explored post-training robustness to synthetically introduced error in verifiable rewards (Plesner et al., 2026; Cai et al., 2025), we examine the semi-verifiable domain where imperfect verifiers are used in practice for rubrics as rewards.

This paper evaluates verifier selection for post-training on semi-verifiable tasks. We compare across model size, dataset domain, evaluation hardness (hard and a mixture of hard and non-hard tasks), reference choice (golden judges), and several verifiers.

Contributions: Across the tested combinations of these settings, we post-train an LLM and measure the performance impact. Across the tested settings, inexpensive verifiers can deliver scores close to the best evaluated training verifier, including in comparisons with strong, expensive candidates such as Grok 4.20. Higher verifier agreement does not always identify the best choice, although very weak verifiers can harm training. For example, the open-weight Gemma 4 31B and 26B verifiers produce some of the strongest training outcomes (Tables 3 and F). We compare two low-cost verifier choices retrospectively, with estimated grading cost reductions of 98.8%98.8\%–99.7%99.7\% relative to the golden grading protocols (Section 4). These reductions would translate to potentially tens of thousands of dollars per training run just for our smaller scale experiments.

2 Methodology

Reinforcement learning (RL), including RL from human feedback (RLHF), RL with verifiable rewards (RLVR), and RL with rubrics as rewards (RLRR) for post-training language models, works by giving rewards based on generated responses. One of the central difficulties in RL lies in shaping these rewards: what you reward and how much. RLVR often focuses on mathematics and coding—domains where answers can be verified deterministically, for example by checking against a known solution. This simplifies outcome verification, but does not by itself determine what to reward or by how much. Besides correctness, one might want to reward style choices, consistency, or reasoning or answer lengths (The Microsoft AI Team, 2026; Xiaomi, 2026). To extend RL post-training to open-ended tasks where correctness is not binary, recent work has turned to rubric-based rewards (Gunjal et al., 2025; Viswanathan et al., 2025). Rubrics decompose a response’s quality into explicit, interpretable criteria, each of which can be assessed by an LLM judge and combined into a scalar reward. This structures the reward signal in a way that generalizes beyond verifiable domains, at the cost of introducing a strong dependency on the quality of the verifier.

2.1 RL with semi-verifiable rewards

RL with semi-verifiable rewards replaces deterministic checks, such as unit tests for code, with a judge’s assessment of rubric criteria. Formally, given an input prompt xi∈𝒟x_{i}\in\mathcal{D}, we generate a response y^i∼πθ(⋅∣xi)\hat{y}_{i}\sim\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x_{i}) from a policy πθ\pi_{\theta}. Each prompt is associated with a rubric Ri={(ci​j,wi​j)}j=1kiR_{i}=\{(c_{ij},w_{ij})\}_{j=1}^{k_{i}}, a set of kik_{i} criteria ci​jc_{ij} with signed weights wi​j∈ℝw_{ij}\in\mathbb{R}.11 1 Positive weights reward responses that satisfy the criterion; negative weights penalize responses that exhibit the behavior described by the criterion. The role of a verifier VϕV_{\phi} is to assess whether a response satisfies each criterion,

Vϕ​(xi,y^i,ci​j)∈{0,1},V_{\phi}(x_{i},\,\hat{y}_{i},\,c_{ij})\;\in\;\{0,1\}, (1)

where 11 indicates that the criterion is met and 00 that it is not. Following the HealthBench scoring convention (Arora et al., 2025), these verdicts are combined into an aggregate reward via a weighted sum,

r(xi,y^i)=∑j=1kiwi​j​Vϕ​(xi,y^i,ci​j)∑j:wi​j>0wi​j≤ 1,r(x_{i},\hat{y}_{i})\;=\;\frac{\sum_{j=1}^{k_{i}}w_{ij}\,V_{\phi}(x_{i},\hat{y}_{i},c_{ij})}{\sum_{j:\,w_{ij}>0}w_{ij}}\;\leq\;1, (2)

where the denominator normalizes by the total positive weight, assumed nonzero, so that a response satisfying all positive criteria and none of the negative ones achieves the maximum reward of 11. PRBench uses a normalized variant seen in Appendix J. The RL objective is then to maximize the expected reward over the training distribution,

maxθ𝔼xi∼𝒟,y^i∼πθ(⋅∣xi)[r(xi,y^i)].\max_{\theta}\;\mathbb{E}_{x_{i}\sim\mathcal{D},\;\hat{y}_{i}\sim\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x_{i})}\!\left[\,r(x_{i},\hat{y}_{i})\,\right]. (3)

As Equations 2 and 3 make clear, verifier errors influence the training reward signal. We study whether agreement with a golden verifier predicts downstream policy performance; we do not characterize which errors cause particular training outcomes.

2.2 The verifier hierarchy

Determining whether a response satisfies a criterion (e.g. correctness, helpfulness, safety) is itself a judgment call that no system can make with perfect fidelity. We formalize this notion through a hierarchy of verifiers, shown in Figure 1.

Oracle verifier. At the top of the hierarchy sits an unattainable oracle V∗V^{*}, a theoretical verifier that returns ground-truth verdicts on every (response, criterion) pair. Human annotators and LLMs approximate V∗V^{*} and can introduce their own noise, biases, and failure modes. For instance, inter- and intra-annotator disagreement are the empirical signatures of human imperfection; analogous inconsistencies arise in LLM-based judges.

Golden verifiers. Prior work has shown that frontier LLMs can match human-to-human agreement on some evaluation tasks (Zheng et al., 2023; Arora et al., 2025). We use frontier models as golden verifiers VGV_{G}: scalable reference judges that remain imperfect proxies for ground truth. They let us study how training-time verifier choice affects post-training outcomes without requiring human annotation of every response.

Training-time verifiers. We use an LLM-based training-time verifier VMV_{M} to drive the policy gradient. We measure agreement with the golden verifiers, following the reference-judge setup of Liu et al. (2026). Agreement is not ground-truth correctness. The golden verifiers also score the trained policies; their grading cost precluded using them for training. The training pool nevertheless includes strong, expensive models such as Grok 4.20. Using the same references for agreement and policy evaluation defines a common evaluation target, but does not rule out shared judge biases as policy outputs change during training. Verifier alignment is quantified by accuracy, precision, recall, and F1F_{1} between VMV_{M} verdicts and VGV_{G} verdicts on held-out (response, criterion) pairs. For each dataset, these pairs come from a fixed slice of 2020 hard tasks for the hard split, plus 2020 non-hard tasks for the mixed all split. To reduce dependence on any particular reference, we evaluate against three frontier models from different vendors and report averages across them.22 2 We compare against each judge’s labels separately and then average the metrics, rather than combining labels first. We post-train each policy using its assigned training-time verifier to score rollout responses, and use the golden verifiers to score evaluation responses.

We batch multiple criteria in each verifier call and refer to the maximum number of criteria per call as the verifier’s batch size, distinct from the policy-training batch size.

2.3 Experimental setup

We focus our experiments on three task domains: medical, finance, and legal tasks. The medical tasks are from HealthBench (Arora et al., 2025), while the finance and legal tasks are from PRBench (Akyürek et al., 2025).

Data. All the datasets contain subsets labeled as hard. We denote the split with the hard tasks as hard and the split with the remaining as non-hard. We use the hard and 10% of the non-hard tasks for evaluation, and leave the remaining non-hard problems for training (the non-hard are split into training and evaluation using a fixed seed of 42). Per-domain split sizes are listed in Table 1. Some PRBench prompts are very long, so we drop the 3 tasks exceeding 90,00090{,}000 characters to keep prompts and responses within Qwen3’s 32,76832{,}768-token native context (Appendix K); Table 1 reflects this filter.

Trainees are Qwen3 1.7B, 4B, and 8B (Qwen Team, 2025), all initialized from the Hugging Face checkpoints. We vary trainee size on HealthBench; PRBench uses Qwen3 8B.

Training-time verifiers (𝐕𝐌\mathbf{V_{M}}). We tested a wide selection of pretrained models on HealthBench generations from Qwen3 8B on the hard subset; the full screening results for all candidates are in Appendix D. From the 5252 tested models, we select 12 for further experiments. These are: Gemma 4 31B, Gemma 4 26B, GPT oss 120B, GPT oss 20B, Gemini 3 flash preview, Grok 4.20, Qwen3 235B, Ministral 14B, Qwen3 8B (a self-judge for the 8B trainee), Mistral 4 small, Qwen3 Next 80B, and LFM2 24B. API instability and grading cost prevented some runs, including runs with Grok 4.20, from completing. Incomplete runs are excluded from the policy comparisons; candidate coverage therefore varies across domains and trainee sizes. Completed runs with poor or collapsed policies remain in the result tables. All are run at batch=3\textrm{batch}{=}3, thinking=low\textrm{thinking}{=}\texttt{low}.

Golden verifiers (𝐕𝐆\mathbf{V_{G}}). Our headline golden is Claude Opus 4.6 with thinking=medium\textrm{thinking}{=}\texttt{medium} and batch=1\textrm{batch}{=}1 (one criterion per call), which we used for most early experiments. To assess robustness to the choice of VGV_{G}, we additionally run two alternate goldens drawn from different model families: Gemini 3.1 Pro and GPT-5.5, both with the same grading configuration. Re-ranking the twelve VMV_{M} candidates and the trained policies under these alternate golden verifiers is purely an evaluation operation and does not require additional training. Unless stated otherwise, golden-judge results are averaged across all three references, following the approach of Verga et al. (2024). Averaging reduces dependence on any single reference, although the judges may share biases. Alignment metrics between the three golden verifiers, including their agreement with a 22-of-33 majority aggregate, are reported in Appendix E.

To spot-check the reference labels, two human experts in rubric data reviewed 50 HealthBench criteria graded by Opus 4.6. Both reviewers were unable to discern any errors in Opus’s labels. However, this small check does not establish perfect golden-judge accuracy.

Training algorithm and hyperparameters can be found in Appendix B. We use GRPO with within-prompt reward standardization and no effective KL penalty; verifier differences therefore affect learning through normalized advantages.

Policy evaluation. The golden verifiers score trained policies on larger task sets than the agreement slices, and the two are disjoint: 100100 hard and 4040 non-hard HealthBench tasks, and 5353–5555 PRBench tasks per domain. Appendix I gives the exact task sets, how the all split is weighted, and how rubric verdicts become policy scores.

3 Verifier Agreement and Post-training Performance

We first compare verifier agreement with post-training performance across domains and trainee sizes. Detailed per-verifier metrics and policy scores are in Appendices F and G.

3.1 Agreement is informative but does not fully rank training verifiers

Figure 2 compares six dataset–split combinations: HealthBench, PRBench finance, and PRBench legal, each with hard and mixed evaluation sets. Agreement and policy performance can be positively associated without giving identical verifier rankings. For example, Qwen3 8B scores on HealthBench-all are 0.370.37 with GPT oss 20B and 0.460.46 with Grok 4.20, despite GPT oss 20B having higher F1F_{1}; inexpensive Gemma 4 26B scores 0.450.45 (Table 10). The practical result is that low grading cost can coexist with strong training outcomes, rather than that agreement has no predictive value.

Figure 3 shows the comparison across the tested Qwen3 model sizes (up to 8B parameters).

Figure 3 also shows that weak verifiers can harm training: Qwen3 8B trained with LFM2 24B still clears its no-training baseline on HealthBench-hard, whereas Qwen3 1.7B trained with the same verifier falls well below baseline. Failure is not confined to low agreement: the Qwen3 8B training verifier yields below-baseline scores despite F1≈0.76F_{1}\approx 0.76 (Table 9). These outcomes do not establish a universal quality threshold or explain the causes of failure. Here, 1−F11-F_{1} measures disagreement with a reference, not the probability of an incorrect rubric verdict.

3.2 Agreement, verifier capability, and training outcomes

The comparisons support a role for verifier quality without requiring a monotonic ranking by agreement. On HealthBench-hard, LFM2 24B has F1=0.54F_{1}=0.54 and yields low policy scores, whereas Gemma 4 31B and Gemma 4 26B have F1=0.83F_{1}=0.83 and 0.760.76, respectively, and both yield an 8B policy score of 0.340.34 (Table 9). The same table reports GDPval as a separate measure of general model capability (Patwardhan et al., 2025). These comparisons concern particular verifiers and do not isolate a causal effect of either capability or agreement.

Appendix O summarizes the descriptive value of other agreement metrics in the existing results. Accuracy and F1F_{1} explain part of the observed variation in policy scores, and the strongest summary depends on the records included. Thus, evidence that agreement is informative is compatible with our cost finding: inexpensive verifiers can still be among the strongest training choices.

Criterion-level agreement also differs from the signal used for learning. The reward aggregates criteria with signed weights, while GRPO standardizes rewards within each prompt’s rollout group. Unweighted F1F_{1} does not measure whether those weighted rewards give the same relative advantages to competing responses. Our fixed-response screening metrics provide a practical comparison of verifiers, but do not characterize training-time errors as the policy changes. We therefore interpret the per-verifier results as observed cost–performance tradeoffs, without assigning significance to small score gaps or attributing them solely to agreement.

4 Practical Implications for Reducing Post-training Costs

The comparisons in Figure 3 motivate considering verifier cost alongside agreement. We compare two choices identified retrospectively: (1) the cost-reducing Pareto verifier — the cheapest candidate with accuracy ≥0.80\geq 0.80 against the golden judge, falling back to the cheapest if none qualifies; and (2) the balanced Pareto verifier — the fixed choice Gemma 4 26B, selected for its mean post-training score in our candidate pool. Table 19 compares these with other choices, and Figures 4 and 7 show their cost–score tradeoff per dataset and on average. The balanced choice uses observed training outcomes; it is not an automatic selection rule validated without a post-training sweep, and neither choice guarantees Pareto optimality in a new setting.

We compare the choices using three metrics, each computed per cell (one dataset–split–golden combination), among candidates with a completed run and an available cost estimate: the score gap, the post-training score of the empirically best eligible verifier in the cell minus the score of the pick (lower is better; 00 means the pick recovered the best verifier); the uplift, the fraction of the available post-training improvement over the no-training baseline that the pick captures; and the cost reduction, the fraction of per-task grading cost saved relative to the golden grading protocol. Averaged across all three datasets, both evaluation splits (all and hard), and the three golden judges, the balanced Pareto verifier achieves a +0.010+0.010 score gap, captures 95%95\% of the available uplift, and gives a 98.8%98.8\% cost reduction; the cost-reducing Pareto verifier achieves a +0.027+0.027 score gap, 82%82\% uplift, and a 99.7%99.7\% cost reduction (Table 3). The cheaper choice has a larger score gap, including 0.0620.062 (6.2 points) on HealthBench-all, where it captures 46%46\% of the available uplift.

These are estimates of verifier API cost under the recorded grading protocols and pricing snapshot, not reductions in total training cost. They depend on model prices (including fallback estimates where prices were unavailable), caching, and batching; golden judges grade one criterion per call, while training verifiers grade up to three. We did not train a policy with a golden verifier, so the golden-cost comparison does not establish equivalent policy quality. Appendix M reports judge calls and tokens per task.

Where the grading savings come from.

Table 2 separates grading resource use from dollar cost on the HealthBench cost probe. The golden protocols require 2.7×2.7\times as many calls as the training-verifier protocols, but call reduction alone does not explain the price difference. Claude Opus 4.6 uses about 3.9×3.9\times as many total tokens as Gemma 4 26B while costing about 296×296\times as much on this probe. Under a matched batch=3\textrm{batch}{=}3, thinking=low\textrm{thinking}{=}\texttt{low} protocol, the token ratio falls to 1.44×1.44\times (Appendix M). Lower token prices therefore account for most of the observed dollar savings.

Self-hosting offers a complementary cost measure: Gemma 4 26B grades a HealthBench rollout in about 0.510.51 H100-seconds, equivalent to roughly 1414 H100-hours for 96,00096{,}000 rollouts at this measured rate. These measurements make the source of the savings concrete while keeping API pricing separate from policy quality and total training cost. Actual training bills also depend on response-length growth and cache reuse. The probe supports comparison at a fixed operating point; the per-domain cost–score results remain the basis for comparing training verifiers.

5 Related Work

Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards

Recent work has focused on scaling model capabilities through RL (Silver & Sutton, 2025; OpenAI, 2024; Zeng et al., 2025). DeepSeek-R1 (DeepSeek-AI, 2025) using GRPO (Shao et al., 2024) is a key example of how RL can be used to cost-effectively increase frontier model capabilities by training on problems with verifiable rewards, such as mathematics and coding, where there is less risk of reward hacking.

Rubrics as rewards beyond verifiable domains.

The post-training literature is migrating from deterministic verifiers (math, code) to LLM judges scoring weighted rubrics in domains where ground truth is undefined. Gunjal et al. (2025) introduce Rubrics-as-Rewards on synthetic medical data and show uplift on HealthBench; Viswanathan et al. (2025) show weighted checklists outperform reward models; Zhou et al. (2025) use rubrics as exploration scaffolds; He et al. (2025) build AdvancedIF for instruction following; and Su et al. (2025) extend RLVR to medicine, chemistry, and economics. In every case, the LLM judge replaces the deterministic verifier, raising the open question we address: how good the verifier needs to be.

Imperfect verifiers and noisy rewards in RLVR.

Recent work has explored how much noise RLVR can tolerate while still giving a large uplift. Plesner et al. (2026) showed that, with symmetric synthetic noise on coding unit tests, RLVR keeps mean validation reward within about 11 point of the clean baseline at a fixed late checkpoint for noise rates up to 20%20\%. Related work derives bias-corrected GRPO estimators under stochastic-channel reward noise: Cai et al. (2025) (asymmetric false-positive/false-negative), Mansouri et al. (2025) (unbiased Bernoulli correction), and Rad et al. (2026) (a Youden’s-J phase transition). Shao et al. (2025) reported the counterintuitive results that Qwen2.5-Math can learn from purely random rewards. Follow-up work by Zhu & Kang (2026) and Chen et al. (2026) attribute the effect to clipping bias and contamination.

LLM-as-Judge meta-evaluation.

We measure each candidate verifier’s agreement (precision, recall, F1 score, and Spearman ρ\rho) with a frontier LLM acting as the operational golden reference, following Zheng et al. (2023). Standard judge benchmarks include RewardBench (Lambert et al., 2025), JudgeBench (Tan et al., 2024), and the rubric-specific RubricEval (Pan et al., 2026); Gu et al. (2026) catalog the inherited biases (position, length, prompt-phrasing, self-preference). Gao et al. (2023) establish that proxy-reward accuracy and gold-reward outcomes can diverge under optimization. Wen et al. (2025) and Kim et al. (2025) study why reward-model evaluation metrics can imperfectly predict downstream policy performance. We extend this empirical question to the cost and training outcomes of rubric-based verifiers across three professional domains.

Cost-aware judge and verifier selection.

Salinas et al. (2025) tune LLM-judge design decisions to reduce evaluation cost by three orders of magnitude. Dorner et al. (2025) prove a hard limit: a judge no stronger than the system it grades cannot reduce the number of required ground-truth labels by more than a factor of two. Liu et al. (2026) compare multiple reasoning and non-reasoning training judges under a single fixed gold-standard reference, and show that trained policies can exploit judge biases. Our study compares off-the-shelf rubric verifiers across grading costs, three professional domains, and three golden references.

6 Conclusions and Future Work

Across the tested rubric-based post-training tasks, inexpensive verifiers can deliver strong policy scores within a candidate pool that includes strong, expensive models. Open-weight Gemma verifiers provide particularly favorable observed cost–score tradeoffs. Agreement remains informative, as illustrated by LFM2’s weak results, but does not fully determine the ranking of training outcomes. Our cost claim concerns the performance achieved by selected inexpensive verifiers in these experiments; it does not require agreement to be uncorrelated with performance or all verifiers to be interchangeable. Understanding which response-level errors affect learning could improve selection beyond aggregate agreement metrics.

7 Limitations

Unstable vendor APIs, several of which went down during this research, and limited post-training compute constrained the number of judges and experiments. Our results cover Qwen3 trainees up to 8B and one GRPO setup; they do not establish generalization to other model families, algorithms, KL settings, or longer training horizons. Hyperparameters were not tuned separately for weaker verifiers.

Within the available compute and grading budget, we evaluated a broad set of verifiers, domains, and trainee sizes. Some configurations were launched more than once, but these repeats were not controlled seed replications (one changed the verifier-serving backend). The reported comparisons therefore describe observed outcomes and do not separate training randomness from verifier effects. Evaluation uses subsets of the held-out pools; task resampling would address evaluation-sample variability, but would not estimate training-seed uncertainty.

Golden-verifier judgments remain LLM references rather than human ground truth, and screening agreement is measured on fixed responses rather than each trained policy’s outputs. We did not train with a golden verifier or conduct a dedicated test of exploitable verifier biases and reward hacking (see Appendix H for observed response-length drift). The cost–quality choices are retrospective and depend on the candidate pool; Appendix O compares other agreement summaries, but we do not establish a generally superior selection metric.

Appendix A Reproducibility

We have approval to open-source the code, benchmarks, and experimental results for the camera-ready version of this paper.

Appendix B Training details

We use GRPO (Shao et al., 2024), with advantages centered and normalized by the within-prompt group’s standard deviation: 88 rollouts per prompt, 120120 prompts per batch, 5×10−65{\times}10^{-6} constant LR, no effective KL penalty, sampling temperature 1.01.0, with eval every 55 rollout steps.

B.1 Rubric-based RLVR on HealthBench

Each HealthBench prompt xx comes with a rubric ℛ⁡(x)={(ck,wk)}k=1Kx\mathcal{R}(x)=\{(c_{k},w_{k})\}_{k=1}^{K_{x}} of KxK_{x} criterion strings ckc_{k} and weights wk∈ℤ∖{0}w_{k}\in\mathbb{Z}\setminus\{0\} (positive weights reward presence; negative weights reward absence). A response yy is scored by submitting each (x,y,ck)(x,y,c_{k}) triple to a judge JJ, which returns a binary verdict Jk​(x,y)∈{0,1}J_{k}(x,y)\in\{0,1\} for whether the criterion is met. The per-task score is the weight-normalized aggregate

sJ​(x,y)=∑k=1Kxwk⋅𝟏​[Jk​(x,y)]∑k=1Kxmax⁡(0,wk),s_{J}(x,y)=\frac{\sum_{k=1}^{K_{x}}w_{k}\cdot\mathbf{1}[J_{k}(x,y)]}{\sum_{k=1}^{K_{x}}\max(0,w_{k})}, (4)

following the convention of Arora et al. (2025): positive-weight criteria add points when met, and negative-weight criteria subtract points when met. We use sJ​(x,y)s_{J}(x,y) as the reward for rollout yy.

PRBench (Akyürek et al., 2025) uses a different per-task aggregate, derived from the same per-criterion verdicts but with a clipped/normalized formula in place of the signed fraction above. We use the PRBench normalized score sJnorm∈[0,1]s_{J}^{\textrm{norm}}\in[0,1] as the reward signal for PRBench training runs. We compute both metrics in the logs which can be found in the supplementary material.

Training uses GRPO with group-standard-deviation normalization, 88 rollouts per prompt, batch size 120120, learning rate 5×10−65{\times}10^{-6}, no effective KL penalty, and a maximum response length of 50005000 tokens; full hyperparameters are in Appendix B. The training-time judge is invoked at batch=3\textrm{batch}{=}3 criteria per call with thinking=low\textrm{thinking}{=}\texttt{low}. This is the configuration whose precision and recall we measure (rather than a more careful single-criterion configuration the same model could in principle support).

B.2 Final hyperparameters

Table 4 reports the hyperparameters used for the headline experiments. The main points are that we (i) use GRPO with group-standard-deviation normalization, (ii) the maximum response length is 50005000 tokens, (iii) the per-prompt rollout count is 88, and (iv) the logged KL coefficient of 0.10.1 does not enter the GRPO objective.

B.3 Training-time judge configuration

The training-time judge is invoked at batch=3\textrm{batch}{=}3 criteria per call, thinking=low\textrm{thinking}{=}\texttt{low}, 11 generation per call, with structured-output JSON returning an ordered verdicts list; single-criterion calls return explanation and criteria_met. The prompt is split at the per-criterion boundary so that the introduction-plus-conversation prefix is reusable across criteria within a task. Prompt caching is enabled where the provider supports it.

B.4 Computational resources and software

We train on a cluster with 8 nodes and 8 H100 GPUs per node. Each training run uses a single H100 node, and the total logged runtime is 1415 node-hours (about 11.3k H100 GPU-hours of node capacity). Per-run GPU configurations are listed in Table 5. Judges are accessed through APIs or hosted locally. The 1415 node-hours cover only policy training. We train on an internal fork of slime (Zhu et al., 2025).

Appendix C Grader prompt

The judge prompt is rendered from one of two Jinja2 templates depending on the batch size: a single-criterion template (Figure 5) used at batch=1\textrm{batch}{=}1 for the golden judge, and a batched template (Figure 6) used at batch=3\textrm{batch}{=}3 for the training-time and candidate-judge runs. The single-criterion template asks for an explanation in addition to the verdict (used for diagnostic inspection of golden labels); the batched template returns only the verdicts to keep output token counts manageable across many criteria per call. Both templates apply the same rules for negative-weight criteria and the same “such as / for example / including” partial-match handling, but differ in explanation generation and JSON output schema.

Caching boundary.

For the batched template we split the rendered prompt at the # Rubric items marker. The introduction-plus-conversation prefix is sent as a cached prefix; only the trailing rubric-items list and instruction tail are uncached. With batch=3\textrm{batch}{=}3, up to three criterion judgments share one call; any additional caching savings depend on provider support and cache reuse.

Appendix D Verifier screening on HealthBench

Before selecting the 1212 training-time verifiers used in the post-training sweep, we screened 5252 candidate models as rubric graders on Qwen3 8B generations from the HealthBench hard subset, measuring their agreement with Claude Opus 4.6 golden labels. Tables 6 and 7 report the full screening results. Agreement accuracy spans 50.9%50.9\% to 95.5%95.5\% and grading cost spans three orders of magnitude, while large portions of the candidate pool are concentrated in the 78%78\%–87%87\% accuracy band; agreement alone does not establish their value for post-training.

The columns are: Batch/Think. — the grading configuration (criteria per call and thinking effort); Acc — agreement accuracy with the golden labels; WAgree — weighted accuracy; Spear. — Spearman correlation with the golden labels; Consist. — self-consistency across repeated gradings; κ\kappa — Cohen’s kappa; YES — fraction of criteria graded as met; Prec/Rec/F1F_{1} — precision, recall, and F1F_{1} vs. the golden labels, treating “criterion met” as the positive class (F1F_{1} was recorded only for candidates short-listed for post-training); Abst. — the fraction of criteria where the model failed to give an answer within three attempts; InTok/OutTok — input and output tokens used for grading; Cost ($) — grading cost in USD; s/task — grading seconds per task; Tested — ✓ marks the 1212 verifiers selected for the post-training sweep. Note that Qwen3 235B A22B thinking abstained on 99.1%99.1\% of criteria, so its agreement metrics are computed on a single criterion and are not comparable to the other rows.

Appendix E Alignment between the golden verifiers

Our results average over three golden verifiers to mitigate single-judge bias. To quantify how much these judges actually disagree, we compare their per-criterion verdicts on a 4040-task HealthBench slice (2020 hard ++ 2020 non-hard tasks, 454454 rubric criteria) graded on Qwen3 8B generations. Each golden grades every criterion three times and we take the within-judge majority verdict, using batch=1\textrm{batch}{=}1, thinking=medium\textrm{thinking}{=}\texttt{medium} for Claude Opus 4.6, GPT-5.5, and Gemini 3.1 Pro.

Table 8 reports the results. Pairwise agreement ranges from 84.4%84.4\% (GPT-5.5 vs. Gemini 3.1 Pro, Cohen’s κ=0.67\kappa=0.67) to 90.8%90.8\% (Claude Opus 4.6 vs. Gemini 3.1 Pro, κ=0.81\kappa=0.81), and all three judges are unanimous on 81.5%81.5\% of criteria. Their overall positive rates are similar (38.5%38.5\%–41.2%41.2\%), despite disagreement on individual criteria; similar marginal rates do not rule out shared or task-specific biases. We also tested aggregating the three frontier judges into a consensus reference by taking the per-criterion 22-of-33 majority vote: Claude Opus 4.6 is highly aligned with this consensus, matching it on 97.1%97.1\% of criteria (κ=0.94\kappa=0.94), versus 93.6%93.6\% for Gemini 3.1 Pro and 90.8%90.8\% for GPT-5.5. (Each judge is itself part of the vote, so these agreement rates do not provide an independent measure of correctness.)

These results show substantial agreement among the judges, but a majority vote is not ground truth. Claude Opus 4.6 agrees with the consensus on 97%97\% of criteria; because it contributes to that consensus, this does not independently validate either reference. Human adjudication of the ∼18%{\sim}18\% of non-unanimous criteria remains a useful direction for future work.

Appendix F HealthBench results

F.1 Verifier agreement and policy scores

Tables 9 and 10 report results for the hard and all splits of HealthBench, covering 12 training-time verifiers and Qwen3 trainees from 1.7B to 8B. Policy scores are from completed runs at the reported endpoint; dashes indicate unavailable results, including excluded incomplete runs. Completed runs with collapsed policies remain in the tables. Some verifiers produce similar scores despite differences in agreement: Qwen3 Next 80B and GPT oss 20B deliver similar 8B policy scores on the hard split despite differences of 16, 20, and 13 percentage points in accuracy, precision, and F1F_{1}, respectively. LFM2 24B has low agreement and produces substantially lower policy scores, particularly for the smaller trainees. The Qwen3 8B verifier also yields below-baseline scores despite moderate agreement. Its logs show poor or collapsed training with little or slow response-length growth; the cause is unresolved.

Appendix G PRBench results

We extend the HealthBench analysis in Appendix F to the two PRBench domains, finance and legal. For each domain we report training-verifier accuracy, precision, recall, F1F_{1}, and Spearman correlation against the golden verifiers, alongside the late-training (rollout step 4949) PRBench score for the trained policy under that training verifier, on both the “all” (hard ++ non-hard) and “hard” evaluation splits.

G.1 Finance

Table 11 reports PRBench-finance results on the “all” split, and Table 12 on the “hard” split. As on HealthBench, higher verifier-level F1F_{1} does not consistently correspond to higher trained-policy scores; both LFM2 24B and GPT oss 120B produce lower scores than several other verifiers.

G.2 Legal

Table 13 reports PRBench-legal results on the “all” split, and Table 14 on the “hard” split. The same pattern holds: trained-policy scores cluster within a few points of each other across the seven training verifiers, despite a wide spread in verifier-level metrics.

Appendix H Response-length drift and collapse

We did not run a dedicated reward-hacking test, but the stored evaluation generations show a common drift. Across the 3232 PRBench evaluation databases, mean response length grows from about 1.91.9k (legal) and 2.42.4k (finance) tokens at step 00 to about 4.94.9k tokens at the final evaluated step, close to the 5,0005{,}000-token cap, and 35%35\%–96%96\% of responses are truncated by the end of training (for example, from 9%9\% to 96%96\% in the finance run trained with GPT oss 120B). This drift occurs with every PRBench training verifier under the shared reward and length setup without an effective KL penalty (Appendix B). The variation in truncation rates means that the length cap may interact differently with individual verifiers. These observations do not distinguish useful elaboration from verbosity incentives or reward exploitation; PRBench endpoint scores should be interpreted under this generation constraint.

The clearest verifier-specific failure is Qwen3 1.7B trained with LFM2 24B on HealthBench. Its mean response length falls from 808808 tokens at step 99 to about one token by step 4949, consistent with its below-baseline scores in Tables 9 and 10.

Appendix I Policy evaluation details

Task sets.

Trained policies are evaluated on 100100 hard and 4040 non-hard HealthBench tasks, 3333 hard and 2020 non-hard PRBench-finance tasks, and 3535 hard and 2020 non-hard PRBench-legal tasks. These sets are larger than, and disjoint from, the 2020/4040-task slices used to compute verifier agreement. For HealthBench, the all score gives each non-hard task four times the weight of a hard task: sall=(100​shard+160​snon-hard)/260s_{\texttt{all}}=(100\,s_{\texttt{hard}}+160\,s_{\texttt{non-hard}})/260. Thus, hard tasks contribute 5/135/13 and non-hard tasks 8/138/13 of the aggregate weight. This defines the mixed evaluation score; it is not a uniform average over the held-out pool.

Run inclusion.

Policy comparisons exclude incomplete training runs and use the stated domain-specific endpoint: rollout step 9999 for HealthBench and 4949 for PRBench. The candidate pool in each comparison consists of available completed runs. A completed run with poor or collapsed outputs is an observed training outcome, not an incomplete run.

Effect of a single grading error.

A policy’s score averages weighted rubric scores rather than binary task outcomes (1111–1818 criteria per task on average; Equations 4 and 5). Flipping one criterion verdict changes its task score by that criterion’s normalized weight and changes the policy score by that amount times the task’s aggregation weight. On HealthBench hard, the absolute change averages 0.000850.00085; the largest change from any single criterion in any of our evaluation sets is 0.01250.0125. These are sensitivity calculations, not uncertainty estimates: they do not account for task sampling, correlated grading errors, stochastic responses, or training-seed variation.

PRBench aggregates.

Main-text scatter plots report the clipped PRBench aggregate, and the tables in Appendix G report the normalized aggregate (Appendix J), so the same run shows different values in the two places. The no-training baselines in those tables are also normalized. PRBench baseline lines are omitted from Figure 2 to avoid comparing normalized baselines with clipped policy scores.

Appendix J PRBench scoring math

PRBench (Akyürek et al., 2025) aggregates per-criterion verdicts Jk​(x,y)∈{0,1}J_{k}(x,y)\in\{0,1\} and weights wkw_{k} via a clipped/normalized formula that differs from HealthBench’s signed-fraction (Equation 4). Let p=∑kwk⋅Jk​(x,y)p=\sum_{k}w_{k}\cdot J_{k}(x,y) be the weighted point total (signed), W+=∑k:wk>0wkW^{+}=\sum_{k:w_{k}>0}w_{k} the sum of positive weights, and W−=∑k:wk<0wk≤0W^{-}=\sum_{k:w_{k}<0}w_{k}\leq 0 the sum of negative weights. Per-task scores are

sJclip​(x,y)=pW+,sJnorm​(x,y)=p−W−W+−W−∈[0,1].s_{J}^{\textrm{clip}}(x,y)=\frac{p}{W^{+}},\qquad s_{J}^{\textrm{norm}}(x,y)=\frac{p-W^{-}}{W^{+}-W^{-}}\in[0,1]. (5)

Dataset-level aggregates are sclip¯=max⁡(0,𝔼⁡[sJclip])\overline{s^{\textrm{clip}}}=\max(0,\mathbb{E}\,[s_{J}^{\textrm{clip}}]) (floor on the mean only) and snorm¯=𝔼⁡[sJnorm]\overline{s^{\textrm{norm}}}=\mathbb{E}\,[s_{J}^{\textrm{norm}}]. We use sJnorms_{J}^{\textrm{norm}} as the GRPO reward signal in PRBench training to keep r⁡(x,y)∈[0,1]r(x,y)\in[0,1].

Appendix K PRBench filtering and lengths

Prompt-length distribution legal.

PRBench-legal prompts are heavily long-tailed: the median is sub-1.21.2k chars but the top ∼5%{\sim}5\% sits in the 3535–8080k char range. Empirical chars-per-token on legal text (numbers, code, citations) is ∼3.4{\sim}3.4 rather than the 4.04.0 typical of English prose. Table 15 summarizes the distribution.

Filter dropouts legal.

The 90,00090{,}000-char input filter (a ∼7{\sim}7k-token safety margin under Qwen3’s 32,76832{,}768-token native context, after accounting for chat-template overhead) drops one outlier from hard: 28de36347e0efacd0188b67e (99,21299{,}212 chars; ∼29{\sim}29k tokens). non-hard and non-hard-eval have no over-the-limit tasks.

Prompt-length distribution: finance.

Table 16 summarizes the post-filter distribution; the same long-tailed pattern holds as for PRBench-legal.

Filter dropouts finance.

The 90,00090{,}000-char filter drops two finance outliers: 992c616d92c1f3a48611eb8a from hard (132,961132{,}961 chars; ∼39{\sim}39k tokens) and 3e4d865a86d6967e36b62740 from non-hard (92,19592{,}195 chars; ∼27{\sim}27k tokens). The remaining splits fit within Qwen3’s 32,76832{,}768-token native context with the 5,0005{,}000-token response-length cap.

Appendix L Cost savings hold across all three golden verifiers.

Results are in Table 17. The cost-reducing and balanced Pareto picks both produce substantial cost reductions regardless of which model is used as the golden eval labeler. The balanced pick achieves the lowest absolute score gap on 55 of 66 slices; the cost-reducing rule (cheapest with accuracy ≥0.80\geq 0.80) produces the higher cost reduction on every slice. Cost reduction is the fraction of per-task verifier cost saved relative to using that cell’s golden as the training-time verifier (geometric mean across the cells in each column); e.g. 99%99\% in column Claude-all means grading 100100 tasks with the chosen verifier costs the same as grading 11 task with Claude Opus on that cell. Splits: all (hard ++ non-hard combined) and hard. Goldens: Claude Opus, Gemini 3.1 Pro, GPT-5.5. Metrics, selectors, and bolding rule as in Table 3.

Appendix M Cost in provider-independent units

Dollar costs depend on provider prices, so Table 18 also reports judge calls and tokens per HealthBench task. The units come from a cost probe that grades 1010 tasks per split once through the same grading code used for training and evaluation. This probe averages the two split means with hard/non-hard weights of 1:41{:}4 (11.611.6 criteria per task on average). These cost-probe weights differ from the 5:85{:}8 aggregate weights of the policy-evaluation all score in Appendix I; the table describes grading resource use on the probe mixture.

Under these protocols, the golden verifiers use 2.7×2.7\times as many calls and 2.82.8–3.9×3.9\times as many tokens per task as the two chosen training verifiers. Most of the 98.8%98.8\%–99.7%99.7\% dollar reduction therefore comes from lower per-token prices rather than fewer tokens; under a matched batch=3\textrm{batch}{=}3, thinking=low\textrm{thinking}{=}\texttt{low} protocol, Claude Opus 4.6 uses only 1.44×1.44\times as many tokens as Gemma 4 26B. Two prices carry additional uncertainty: the GPT oss 20B price was the billed price on one provider, about 3×3\times below the list price in our price file, and the Gemma 4 26B cost uses a fallback list price because the provider did not report one. When self-hosted, Gemma 4 26B grades a HealthBench rollout in about 0.510.51 H100-seconds, or roughly 1414 H100-hours for the ≈96{\approx}96k rollouts of a 100100-step run (120120 prompts ×\times 88 rollouts ×\times 100100 steps).

Appendix N Verifier-selection strategy audit

Figure 7 summarizes mean cost and policy score over the available evaluation cells for each plotted verifier. There are up to 1818 cells (33 datasets ×\times 22 splits ×\times 33 goldens, Qwen3 8B trainee); coverage depends on available completed runs. In particular, LFM2 24B has no legal result and covers only 1212 cells. The two highlighted choices have favorable plotted cost–score tradeoffs, but means over different domain coverage do not establish dominance on a common task mixture. The per-domain comparisons and cell-wise selection summaries provide the corresponding comparisons within each available candidate pool.

We evaluated 2020 verifier-selection strategies for the bivariate (cost,post-training score)(\text{cost},\,\text{post-training score}) Pareto optimization task; Table 19 reports the aggregate result of each. The balanced Pareto choice is the fixed Gemma 4 26B verifier selected retrospectively from policy outcomes. The strategies and thresholds are compared on these same cells, so the audit is descriptive and does not estimate selection performance on new candidate pools. Strategies fall into three families: (i) quality-first rules that always pick a single verifier or argmax over a quality metric; (ii) cost-first rules that take the cheapest verifier above a quality floor (with fallback to the cheapest if no verifier meets the floor); and (iii) balanced rules that combine cost and quality into a single selection score.

Each strategy is applied to candidates with completed runs and available cost estimates in each of 1818 evaluation cells (33 datasets ×\times 22 splits ×\times 33 goldens; trainee Qwen3 8B). These cells reuse training runs and overlapping evaluation sets, and are not 1818 independent training replications. Results are aggregated using the same definitions as Table 3: Score gap is the post-training score difference to the empirically best eligible verifier per cell (lower is better); Uplift is the fraction of available post-training improvement captured relative to the no-training baseline (100%100\% matches the empirical best, 0%0\% matches no training); Cost reduction is the geometric mean across cells of 1−(picked verifier cost/golden cost)1-(\text{picked verifier cost}/\text{golden cost}) per task; Pareto is the fraction of the 1818 cells in which the strategy’s pick lies on the empirical (cost,score)(\text{cost},\,\text{score}) Pareto frontier. Strategies are sorted by mean Uplift descending. The two paper picks — the balanced Pareto verifier (quality-first) and the cost-reducing Pareto verifier (cost-first) — illustrate the trade-off, with the balanced pick achieving the lowest score gap and highest Uplift in the entire pool, and the cost-reducing pick (cheapest with accuracy ≥0.80\geq 0.80) delivering greater grading cost reduction while retaining 17/1817/18 Pareto coverage.

Appendix O Agreement summaries as predictors of post-training score

In an exploratory analysis of the results table, we added one agreement summary at a time to a linear model with trainee, domain, split, and golden-judge indicators, and recorded its incremental R2R^{2}. A model with training-verifier identity indicators provides a descriptive comparison for the amount of variation associated with verifier choice. It is not a formal upper bound for summaries that vary across domains, splits, or golden judges.

Excluding the Qwen3 8B training verifier (396396 records), verifier identity adds Δ​R2=0.255\Delta R^{2}=0.255. Accuracy is the strongest single summary (0.1650.165, about 65%65\% of the increment from verifier identity), and F1F_{1} adds 0.1190.119 (47%47\%). Self-consistency across repeated gradings is the weakest summary tested (0.0020.002). Restricting to the Qwen3 8B trainee (252252 records, including the self-judge), verifier identity adds 0.4340.434. The best single summaries there are the fraction of criteria graded as met, balanced accuracy, and false-positive rate (0.0390.039–0.0430.043), compared with 0.0300.030 for F1F_{1}, 0.0110.011 for false-negative rate, and 0.0040.004 for calibration bias.

Agreement summaries therefore capture part, but not all, of the observed differences between training verifiers, and which summary ranks first depends on the records included. These are in-sample descriptive fits, not held-out predictions. The records share training runs and are not independent, so we do not attach significance tests to these comparisons or treat their record counts as numbers of independent experiments.
